title: Texas H-1B Freeze at Public Universities Puts Indian Academics at Risk
excerpt: Governor Abbott's order halting new H-1B petitions at state agencies and universities through May 2027 is reshaping academic hiring in America's second-largest state.
body:
• Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered all public universities and state agencies to freeze new H-1B visa petitions until May 31, 2027, requiring written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission for any exceptions
  • Indians make up roughly 71% of all approved H-1B applications nationally, making the freeze particularly impactful for Indian academics and researchers seeking positions in Texas
  • Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has launched parallel investigations into H-1B "ghost offices" in North Texas, while Florida is pursuing similar restrictions under Governor DeSantis
  • Immigration experts warn the freeze could trigger a brain drain from Texas universities, pushing top talent to the 49 other states or abroad

Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered all public universities and state agencies to immediately halt new H-1B visa petitions in January, imposing a freeze that will last through May 31, 2027, and raising alarm among the foreign-born researchers and academics who have helped build the state's research reputation.

The directive bars any state agency or public university from initiating or filing new H-1B visa petitions without written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission. Abbott framed the order as a corrective to what he called abuse of the visa program.

"State government must lead by example and ensure that employment opportunities — particularly those funded with taxpayer dollars — are filled by Texans first."

— Governor Greg Abbott

What the Freeze Requires

Beyond halting new petitions, the order mandates detailed reporting. State agencies and public universities were required to submit information to the Texas Workforce Commission by March 27, including the number of new and renewed H-1B petitions filed in 2025, job classifications and descriptions, countries of origin of visa holders, visa expiration dates, and documentation showing efforts to give qualified Texans a reasonable opportunity to apply for positions filled by H-1B workers.

The directive does not appear to apply to renewals or extensions of status for workers already employed at these institutions — a distinction that offers some relief to currently sponsored employees but does nothing for prospective hires.

In a radio interview, Abbott was blunt about his expectations. "I don't see any reason why we need any H-1B visa employees in our public schools in the state of Texas," he said.

Impact on Indian Professionals

Indians make up an estimated 71% of all approved H-1B applications in recent years, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services data. The major fields — technology, engineering, medicine, and research — overlap significantly with the roles universities typically sponsor. For Indian academics seeking positions at Texas public universities, the freeze effectively closes a door that was already narrowing under federal-level restrictions.

"The people will have to go home, or have to leave or find a job in another state," said Faye Kolly, an Austin immigration attorney and founding partner of McChesney Kolly. "Our best state institutions, universities, will have trouble recruiting people, because they can just go elsewhere. They can go to 49 other states, or outside of the U.S. for that matter."

Texas State University, one of the state's public institutions, confirmed it was complying with the directive. "Texas State University is aware of the letter issued today by Governor Greg Abbott regarding the H-1B directives," spokesperson Jayme Blaschke said. "The university is reviewing the order, addressing the questions raised, and taking steps to ensure compliance with all applicable requirements."

A Pattern Across States

The Texas freeze does not exist in isolation. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has pushed to restrict H-1B visas for professors at state universities, alleging they are used to import "cheap foreign labor." The Florida Board of Governors has been considering a proposal to ban hiring faculty with H-1B visas for one year.

At the federal level, the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions from abroad has already depressed applications nationally. Registrations for the FY2026 H-1B lottery dropped by as much as 43% from the prior year, according to estimates cited by Bloomberg Law — the lowest since the online lottery system started in 2020.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has separately launched investigations into alleged H-1B fraud, targeting North Texas businesses suspected of operating "ghost offices" — sham companies used to sponsor visa workers. "Any criminal who attempts to scam the H-1B visa program and use 'ghost offices' or other fraudulent ploys should be prepared to face the full force of the law," Paxton said.

The Academic Cost

"What has made U.S. higher education the best in the world is that we have been able to attract the best people for these positions," said Miriam Feldblum, CEO of the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration. With 12 public R-1 research universities, Texas has the second-highest number of H-1B visa holders among state university systems in the country, behind California.

Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University, offered a more political reading of the directive: "Since Governor Abbott can't force Texas private companies to stop using the H-1B visa program, this is a way for him to signal to Republicans in Texas he is doing everything in his power to fight H-1B visa abuse."

For Indian professionals weighing academic positions in the United States, the message from Texas is clear: the state's public universities are off-limits for new H-1B sponsorship, at least until May 2027 — and the broader climate suggests the restrictions may not stop there.
nri_angle: Indians make up 71% of H-1B recipients nationally, and the Texas freeze directly affects Indian academics, researchers, and professionals seeking university positions in the state.
